  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item $Y$ is compact.
    \item any continuous function from $Y \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded.
    \item $Y$ is not an open subset of $X$.
    \item none of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function and let $S$ be a non-empty proper subset of $\mathbb{R}$. Which one of the following statements is always true? (Here $\overline{A}$ denotes the closure of $A$ and $A^\circ$ denotes the interior of $A$.)
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item $f(S)^\circ \subseteq f(S^\circ)$
    \item $f(\overline{S}) \subseteq \overline{f(S)}$
    \item $f(\overline{S}) \supseteq \overline{f(S)}$
    \item $f(S)^\circ \supseteq f(S^\circ)$.
  \end{enumerate}

What is the last digit of $97^{2013}$?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item $1$
    \item $3$
    \item $7$
    \item $9$.
  \end{enumerate}

For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ we define $s_n = 1^3 + 2^3 + 3^3 + \dots + n^3$. Which of the following holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item $s_n$ is an odd integer.
    \item $s_n = n^2(n + 1)^2 / 4$.
    \item $s_n = n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6$.
    \item none of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $f: [0, 1] \to [0, \infty)$ be continuous. Suppose $\int_0^x f(t)\,dt \ge f(x)$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$. Then
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item no such function exists.
    \item there are infinitely many such functions.
    \item there is only one such function.
    \item there are exactly two such functions.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be a continuous map such that $f(x) = 0$ for only finitely many values of $x$. Which of the following is true?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item either $f(x) \le 0$ for all $x$, or $f(x) \ge 0$ for all $x$.
    \item the map $f$ is onto.
    \item the map $f$ is one-to-one.
    \item none of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $S_n$ be the symmetric group of $n$ letters. There exists an onto group homomorphism
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item from $S_5$ to $S_4$
    \item from $S_4$ to $S_2$
    \item from $S_5$ to $\mathbb{Z}/5$
    \item from $S_4$ to $\mathbb{Z}/4$.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $H_1, H_2$ be two distinct subgroups of a finite group $G$, each of order $2$. Let $H$ be the smallest subgroup containing $H_1$ and $H_2$. Then the order of $H$ is
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item always $2$
    \item always $4$
    \item always $8$
    \item none of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Which of the following groups are isomorphic?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$
    \item $\mathbb{R}^*$ and $\mathbb{C}^*$
    \item $S_3 \times \mathbb{Z}/4$ and $S_4$
    \item $\mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathbb{Z}/4$.
  \end{enumerate}

The number of irreducible polynomials of the form $x^2 + ax + b$ with $a, b$ in the field $\mathbb{F}_7$ of $7$ elements is:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item $7$
    \item $21$
    \item $35$
    \item $49$.
  \end{enumerate}

$X$ is a topological space of infinite cardinality which is homeomorphic to $X \times X$. Then
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item $X$ is not connected.
    \item $X$ is not compact.
    \item $X$ is not homeomorphic to a subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
    \item none of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $X$ be a non-empty topological space such that every function $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous. Then
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item $X$ has the discrete topology.
    \item $X$ has the indiscrete topology.
    \item $X$ is compact.
    \item $X$ is not connected.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $f: X \to Y$ be a continuous map between metric spaces. Then $f(X)$ is a complete subset of $Y$ if
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\Alph*.]
    \item the space $X$ is compact.
    \item the space $Y$ is compact.
    \item the space $X$ is complete.
    \item the space $Y$ is complete.
  \end{enumerate}
Every countable group $G$ has only countably many distinct subgroups.
Any automorphism of the group $(\mathbb{Q}, +)$ under addition is of the form $x \mapsto qx$ for some $q \in \mathbb{Q}$.
The equation $x^3 + 3x - 4 = 0$ has exactly one real root.
The equation $x^3 + 10x^2 - 100x + 1729 = 0$ has at least one complex root $\alpha$ such that $|\alpha| > 12$.
All non-trivial proper subgroups of $(\mathbb{R}, +)$ are cyclic.
Every infinite abelian group has at least one element of infinite order.
If $A$ and $B$ are similar matrices then every eigenvector of $A$ is an eigenvector of $B$.
If a real square matrix $A$ is similar to a diagonal matrix and satisfies $A^n = 0$ for some $n$, then $A$ must be the zero matrix.
There is an element of order $51$ in the multiplicative group $(\mathbb{Z}/103\mathbb{Z})^*$.
Any normal subgroup of order $2$ is contained in the center of the group.
Consider the sequences $x_n = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{j}$ and $y_n = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{j^2}$. Then $\{x_n\}$ is Cauchy but $\{y_n\}$ is not.

Let $f: [a, b] \to [c, d]$ and $g: [c, d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be Riemann integrable functions defined on the closed intervals $[a, b]$ and $[c, d]$ respectively. Then the composite $g \circ f$ is also Riemann integrable.
Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(x) = \sin x^3$. Then $f$ is continuous but not uniformly continuous.
Let $x_1 \in (0, 1)$ be a real number between $0$ and $1$. For $n \ge 1$, define $x_{n+1} = x_n - x_n^{n+1}$. Then $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n$ exists.
Suppose $\{a_i\}$ is a sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ such that $\sum |a_i||x_i| < \infty$ whenever $\sum |x_i| < \infty$. Then $\{a_i\}$ is a bounded sequence.
Let $P(x) = 1 + x + \frac{x^2}{2!} + \frac{x^3}{3!} + \dots + \frac{x^n}{n!}$ where $n$ is a large positive integer. Then $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{e^x}{P(x)} = 1$.
Every differentiable function $f: (0, 1) \to [0, 1]$ is uniformly continuous.
Consider the function $f(x) = ax + b$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. Then the iteration $x_{n+1} = f(x_n)$, $n \ge 0$, for a given $x_0$ converges to $b/(1 - a)$ whenever $0 < a < 1$.
Every homeomorphism of the $2$-sphere to itself has a fixed point.
Let $X$ be a complete metric space such that distance between any two points is less than $1$. Then $X$ is compact.
There exists a continuous surjective function from $S^1$ onto $\mathbb{R}$.
There exists a complete metric on the open interval $(0, 1)$ inducing the usual topology.
There exists a continuous surjective map from the complex plane onto the non-zero reals.
If every differentiable function on a subset $X \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ (i.e., restriction of a differentiable function on a neighbourhood of $X$) is bounded, then $X$ is compact.
Let $f: X \to Y$ be a continuous map between metric spaces. If $f$ is a bijection, then its inverse is also continuous.

Let $f$ be a function on the closed interval $[0, 1]$ defined by
  \[
    f(x) = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \text{ is rational,} \\ x^2 & \text{if } x \text{ is irrational.} \end{cases}
  \]
  Then $f$ is continuous at $0$ and $1$.
There exists an infinite subset $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ such that any three vectors in $S$ are linearly independent.
The inequality $\sqrt{n+1} - \sqrt{n} < \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ is false for all $n$ such that $101 \le n \le 2000$.
There exists a bijection between $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the open interval $(0, 1)$.
Let $S$ be the set of all sequences $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n, \dots\}$ where each entry $a_i$ is either $0$ or $1$. Then $S$ is countable.
Let $\{a_n\}$ be any non-constant sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ such that $a_{n+1} = \frac{a_n + a_{n+2}}{2}$ for all $n \ge 1$. Then $\{a_n\}$ is unbounded.
The function $f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(n) = n^3 - 3n$ is injective.

Let $V$ be the vector space consisting of polynomials with real coefficients in variable $t$ of degree $< 9$. Let $D: V \to V$ be the linear operator defined by $D(f) := \frac{df}{dt}$. Then $0$ is an eigenvalue of $D$.
If $A$ is a complex $n \times n$ matrix with $A^2 = A$ then $\operatorname{rank} A = \operatorname{trace} A$.
If $H_1$ \& $H_2$ are subgroups of a group $G$ then $H_1 \cdot H_2 = \{h_1 h_2 \in G \mid h_1 \in H_1, \, h_2 \in H_2\}$ is a subgroup of $G$.
There exist polynomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$, with complex coefficients, such that $\left(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right)^2 = x$.
Let $f$ be real valued, differentiable on $(a, b)$ and $f'(x) \ne 0$ for all $x \in (a, b)$. Then $f$ is $1$--$1$.
Every subgroup of order $74$ in a group of order $148$ is normal.

Let $u_1, u_2, u_3, u_4$ be vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $u = \sum_{j=1}^4 t_j u_j$; $t_j > 0$ and $\sum_{j=1}^4 t_j = 1$. Then three vectors $v_1, v_2, v_3 \in \mathbb{R}^2$ may be chosen from $\{u_1, u_2, u_3, u_4\}$ such that $u = \sum_{j=1}^3 s_j v_j$, $s_j \ge 0$, $\sum_{j=1}^3 s_j = 1$.
The inequality $\sqrt{1 + x} < 1 + x/2$ for $x \in (-1, 10)$ is true.
If $n$ is not a multiple of $23$ then the remainder when $n^{11}$ is divided by $23$ is $\pm 1 \pmod{23}$.
Suppose $A$ is a nilpotent matrix and $I$ is the identity matrix. Then $(I + A)$ is invertible.

The equations
  \begin{align*}
    x_1 + \frac{1}{2} x_2 + \frac{1}{3} x_3 &= 1 \\
    x_1 + \frac{1}{4} x_2 + \frac{1}{9} x_3 &= 1 \\
    x_1 + \frac{1}{8} x_2 + \frac{1}{27} x_3 &= 1
  \end{align*}
  have no solution.
Let $V$ be the vector space consisting of polynomials of $\mathbb{R}[t]$ of $\deg \le 2$. The map $T: V \to V$ sending $f(t)$ to $f(t) + f'(t)$ is invertible.
Let $P$ be an $n \times n$ matrix whose row sums equal $1$. Then for any positive integer $m$ the row sums of the matrix $P^m$ equal $1$.
There is a non trivial group homomorphism from $\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{R}$.
If the equation {[obscured in source]} holds in a {[obscured in source]} $yzx = 1$.
Any $3 \times 3$ and $5 \times 5$ skew-symmetric matrices have always zero determinants.
The number $2$ is a prime in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$.
Let $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function. Then the derivative $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y}$ can exist without $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ existing.
If $f$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$ and if $\int_0^1 f(x) x^n\,dx = 0$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$, then $\int_0^1 f^2(x)\,dx = 0$.
If $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ and open then the interior of the closure $\overline{A}^\circ$ is $A$.
If $f \in C^\infty$ and $f^{(k)}(0) = 0$ for all integer $k \ge 0$, then $f \equiv 0$.
Let $f: [0, 1] \to [0, 1]$ be continuous then $f$ assumes the value $\int_0^1 f^2(t)\,dt$ somewhere in $[0, 1]$.
Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ {[obscured in source]} that $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x - h)}{h}$ exists for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $f$ is differentiable in $\mathbb{R}$.
The functions $f(x) = x|x|$ and $x|\sin x|$ are not differentiable at $x = 0$.
The composition of two uniformly continuous functions need not always be uniformly continuous.
$f: [0, \infty] \to [0, \infty]$ is continuous and bounded then $f$ has a fixed point.

If a rectangle $R := \{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid A \le x \le B, \, C \le y \le D\}$ can be covered (allowing overlaps) by $25$ discs of radius $1$ then it can also be covered by $101$ discs of radius $\frac{1}{2}$.
Given any integer $n \ge 2$, we can always find an integer $m$ such that each of the $n - 1$ consecutive integers $m + 2, m + 3, \dots, m + n$ are composite.
The $10 \times 10$ matrix {[obscured in source; last column $v_1 w_{10}, v_2 w_{10}, \dots, v_{10} w_{10}$]} has rank $2$, where $v_i, w_i \in \mathbb{C}$.
If every continuous function on $X \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is bounded, then $X$ is compact.
The graph of $xy = 1$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$ is connected.

Consider the differential equations (with $y$ a function of $x$):
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y$, $y(0) = 0$,
    \item $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = |y|^{1/3}$, $y(0) = 0$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then (1) has infinitely many solutions but (2) has finite number of solutions.

Consider the sequence $\{x_n\}$ defined by $x_n = \frac{[nx]}{n}$ for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ where $[\,]$ denotes the integer part. Then $\{x_n\}$
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item converges to $x$.
    \item converges but not to $x$.
    \item does not converge.
    \item oscillates.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $A$ be a $5 \times 5$ matrix with real entries, then $A$ has
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item an eigenvalue which is purely imaginary.
    \item at least one real eigenvalue.
    \item at least two eigenvalues which are not real.
    \item at least $2$ distinct real eigenvalues.
  \end{enumerate}

The groups $\mathbb{Z}_9$ and $\mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_3$ are
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item isomorphic
    \item abelian
    \item non abelian
    \item cyclic
  \end{enumerate}

The differential equation $\displaystyle \frac{dy}{dx} = y^{1/3}$, $y(0) = 0$ has
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item a unique solution.
    \item no nontrivial solution.
    \item finite number of solutions.
    \item infinite number of solutions.
  \end{enumerate}

The function $f_n(x) = n \sin(x/n)$
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item does not converge for any $x$ as $n \to \infty$.
    \item converges to the constant function $1$ as $n \to \infty$.
    \item converges to the function $x$ as $n \to \infty$.
    \item does not converge for all $x$ as $n \to \infty$.
  \end{enumerate}

The equation $x^{22} \equiv 2 \pmod{23}$ has
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item no solutions.
    \item $23$ solutions.
    \item exactly one solution.
    \item $22$ solutions.
  \end{enumerate}

The sum of the squares of the roots of the cubic equation $x^3 - 4x^2 + 6x + 1 = 0$ is
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $0$.
    \item $4$.
    \item $16$.
    \item none of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

The function $f(x)$ defined by
  \[
    f(x) = \begin{cases} ax + b, & x \ge 1, \\ x^2 + 3x + 3, & x \le 1 \end{cases}
  \]
  is {[obscured in source]}
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item for a unique value of $a$ and infinitely many values of $b$.
    \item for a unique value of $b$ and infinitely many values of $a$.
    \item for infinitely many values of $a$ and $b$.
    \item none of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $m \le n$ be natural numbers. The number of injective maps from a set of cardinality $m$ to a set of cardinality $n$ is
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $m!$
    \item $n!$
    \item $(n - m)!$
    \item none of the above.
  \end{enumerate}
\emph{(True/False)} For any real number $c$, the polynomial $x^3 + x + c$ has exactly one real root.
\emph{(True/False)} $A$ is a $3 \times 4$-matrix of rank $3$. Then the system of equations $Ax = b$ has exactly one solution.
\emph{(True/False)} If $A, B$ are closed subsets of $[0, \infty)$, then $A + B = \{x + y \mid x \in A, \, y \in B\}$ is closed in $[0, \infty)$.
\emph{(True/False)} The polynomial $x^4 + 7x^3 - 13x^2 + 11x$ has exactly one real root.
\emph{(True/False)} The value of the infinite product $\displaystyle \prod_{n=2}^\infty \left(1 - \frac{1}{n^2}\right)$ is $1$.

\emph{(True/False)} Consider the map $T$ from the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $5$ over the reals to $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$, given by sending a polynomial $P$ to the pair $(P(3), P'(3))$ where $P'$ is the derivative of $P$. Then the dimension of the kernel is $3$.
\emph{(True/False)} The derivative of the function $\displaystyle \int_0^{\sqrt{x}} e^{-t^2}\,dt$ at $x = 1$ is $e^{-1}$.
\emph{(True/False)} The equation $63x + 70y + 15z = 2010$ has an integral solution.
\emph{(True/False)} Any continuous function from the open unit interval $(0, 1)$ to itself has a fixed point.
\emph{(True/False)} There exists a group with a proper subgroup isomorphic to itself.
\emph{(True/False)} The space of solutions of infinitely differentiable functions satisfying the equation $y'' + y = 0$ is infinite dimensional.

\emph{(True/False)} The function
  \[
    f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x \text{ is rational,} \\ x & \text{if } x \text{ is irrational} \end{cases}
  \]
  is not continuous anywhere on the real line.
Let $A$ be a $2 \times 2$-matrix with complex entries. The number of $2 \times 2$-matrices $A$ with complex entries satisfying the equation $A^3 = A$ is infinite.
In the ring $\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}$ the equation $x^2 = 1$ has exactly $2$ solutions.
There are $n$ homomorphisms from the group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ to the additive group of rationals.
A bounded continuous function on $\mathbb{R}$ is uniformly continuous.
The symmetric group $S_5$ consisting of permutations on $5$ symbols has an element of order $6$.
Suppose $f_n(x)$ is a sequence of {[obscured in source]} on the closed interval $[0, 1]$ converging to $0$ pointwise. {[obscured in source]} converges to $0$.
If $A$ and $B$ are $3 \times 3$ matrices and $A$ is invertible, then there exists an integer $n$ such that $A + nB$ is invertible.
Let $P$ be a degree $3$ polynomial with complex coefficients such that the constant term is $2010$. Then $P$ has a root $\alpha$ with $|\alpha| > 10$.

Suppose a box contains three cards, one with both sides white, one with both sides black, and one with one side white and the other side black. If you pick a card at random, and the side facing you is white, then the probability that the other side is white is $1/2$.
There exists a set $A \subset \{1, 2, \dots, 100\}$ with $65$ elements, such that $65$ cannot be expressed as a sum of two elements in $A$.
Let $S$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$ such that any three elements in $S$ span a two dimensional subspace. Then $S$ spans a two dimensional space.
Any non-singular $k \times k$-matrix with real entries can be made singular by changing exactly one entry.
Let $f$ be a continuous integrable function of $\mathbb{R}$ such that either $f(x) > 0$ or $f(x) + f(x + 1) > 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\,dx > 0$.
A gardener throws $18$ seeds onto an {[obscured in source]} two seeds are within a distance of $25$ centimetres.

A cyclic group of order $60$ has
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $12$ generators.
    \item $15$ generators.
    \item $16$ generators.
    \item $20$ generators.
  \end{enumerate}

Which of the following is false?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item Any abelian group of order $27$ is cyclic.
    \item Any abelian group of order $14$ is cyclic.
    \item Any abelian group of order $21$ is cyclic.
    \item Any abelian group of order $30$ is cyclic.
  \end{enumerate}

The sum of the series $\displaystyle \frac{1}{1 \cdot 2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3} + \frac{1}{3 \cdot 4} + \dots + \frac{1}{100 \cdot 101}$ is
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $\frac{99}{101}$
    \item $\frac{98}{101}$
    \item $\frac{99}{100}$
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $f$ be a one to one function from the closed interval $[0, 1]$ to the set of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$, then
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $f$ must be onto.
    \item range of $f$ must contain a rational number.
    \item range of $f$ must contain an irrational number.
    \item range of $f$ must contain both rational and irrational numbers.
  \end{enumerate}

The maximum value of $f(x) = x^n(1 - x)^n$ for a natural number $n \ge 1$ and $0 \le x \le 1$ is
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $\frac{1}{2^n}$
    \item $\frac{1}{3^n}$
    \item $\frac{1}{5^n}$
    \item $\frac{1}{4^n}$
  \end{enumerate}

Let $f(x) = |x|^{3/2}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Then
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $f$ is uniformly continuous.
    \item $f$ is continuous, but not differentiable at $x = 0$.
    \item $f$ is differentiable and $f'$ is continuous.
    \item $f$ is differentiable, but $f'$ is discontinuous at $x = 0$.
  \end{enumerate}

The total number of subsets of a set of $6$ elements is
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $720$
    \item $6^6$
    \item $21$
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ be the set of $n \times n$-matrices with real entries. Which of the following statements is true?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item Any matrix $A \in M_4(\mathbb{R})$ has a real eigenvalue.
    \item Any matrix $A \in M_5(\mathbb{R})$ has a real eigenvalue.
    \item Any matrix $A \in M_2(\mathbb{R})$ has a real eigenvalue.
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

The series $\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{\sqrt{n}}$
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item converges but not absolutely.
    \item converges absolutely.
    \item diverges.
    \item none of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

The sum of the roots of the equation $x^5 + 3x^2 + 7 = 0$ is
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $-3$
    \item $\frac{3}{7}$
    \item $\frac{-1}{7}$
    \item $0$
  \end{enumerate}

Let $G$ be the set of all $2 \times 2$ symmetric, invertible matrices with real entries. Then with matrix multiplication, $G$ is
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item an infinite group.
    \item a finite group.
    \item not a group.
    \item an abelian group.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $u_n = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right)$ and consider the series $\sum u_n$. Which of the following statements is false?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $\sum u_n$ is convergent.
    \item $u_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.
    \item $\sum u_n$ is divergent.
    \item $\sum u_n$ is absolutely convergent.
  \end{enumerate}

If $V$ is a vector space over the field $\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}}(V) = 3$, then $V$ has
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $125$ elements.
    \item $15$ elements.
    \item $243$ elements.
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

If $f, g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ are uniformly continuous functions, then their composition $g \circ f$ is
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item uniformly continuous.
    \item continuous but not uniformly continuous.
    \item continuous and bounded.
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Which of the following statements is false?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item There exists a natural number which when divided by $3$ leaves remainder $1$ and which when divided by $4$ leaves remainder $0$.
    \item There exists a natural number which when divided by $6$ leaves remainder $2$ and when divided by $9$ leaves remainder $1$.
    \item There exists a natural number which when divided by $7$ leaves remainder $1$ and when divided by $11$ leaves remainder $3$.
    \item There exists a natural number which when divided by $12$ leaves remainder $7$ and when divided by $8$ leaves remainder $3$.
  \end{enumerate}

If $f_n(x)$ are continuous functions from $[0, 1]$ to $[0, 1]$, and $f_n(x) \to f(x)$ as $n \to \infty$, then which of the following statements is true?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $f_n(x)$ converges to $f(x)$ uniformly on $[0, 1]$.
    \item $f_n(x)$ converges to $f(x)$ uniformly on $(0, 1)$.
    \item $f(x)$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$.
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $A, B$ be subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. Define $A + B$ to be the set of all sums $x + y$ with $x \in A$ and $y \in B$. Which of the following statements is false?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item If $A$ and $B$ are bounded, then $A + B$ is bounded.
    \item If $A$ and $B$ are open, then $A + B$ is open.
    \item If $A$ and $B$ are closed, then $A + B$ is closed.
    \item If $A$ and $B$ are connected, then $A + B$ is connected.
  \end{enumerate}

Number of solutions of the ordinary differential equation $\displaystyle \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} - y = 0$; $y(0) = 0$, $y(\pi) = 1$
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item is $0$.
    \item is $1$.
    \item is $2$.
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

The function $f(x)$ defined by
  \[
    f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x \text{ is rational,} \\ x & \text{if } x \text{ is irrational} \end{cases}
  \]
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item is not continuous at any point.
    \item is continuous at every point.
    \item is continuous at every rational number.
    \item is continuous at $x = 0$.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $G = \{z \in \mathbb{C} \mid z^n = 1 \text{ for some positive integer } n\}$. Then under multiplication of complex numbers,
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $G$ is a group of finite order.
    \item $G$ is a group of infinite order, but every element of $G$ has finite order.
    \item $G$ is a cyclic group.
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Let $x$ and $y$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ be non-zero column vectors. Form the matrix $A = x y^t$ where $y^t$ is the transpose of $y$. Then the rank of $A$ is
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $2$
    \item $0$
    \item at least $n/2$.
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Which of the following is true?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is not diagonalisable.
    \item The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is diagonalisable.
    \item The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is diagonalisable.
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

If $n$ and $m$ are positive integers and $n^9 = 19m + r$, then the possible values for $r$ modulo $19$ are
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item only $0$.
    \item only $0, \pm 1$.
    \item only $\pm 1$.
    \item None of the above.
  \end{enumerate}

Define $\{x_n\}$ as $x_1 = 0.1$, $x_2 = 0.101$, $x_3 = 0.101001, \dots$. Then the sequence $\{x_n\}$
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item converges to a rational number.
    \item converges to an irrational number.
    \item does not converge.
    \item oscillates.
  \end{enumerate}

The equations
  \begin{align*}
    x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 &= 1 \\
    x_1 + 4x_2 + 9x_3 &= 1 \\
    x_1 + 8x_2 + 27x_3 &= 1
  \end{align*}
  have
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item only one solution.
    \item two solutions.
    \item infinitely many solutions.
    \item no solution.
  \end{enumerate}

Which of the following statements is false?
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item The polynomial $x^2 + x + 1$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
    \item The polynomial $x^2 - 2$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.
    \item The polynomial $x^2 + 1$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
    \item The polynomial $x^2 + 1$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
  \end{enumerate}
